pages.text: In the southern part of Nigeria, stretching from the coast inland toward the Middle Belt, there is a forest. It is not like any other landscape in Nigeria. It is dense, layered, and perpetually green. It smells of damp earth and rotting leaves and flowering plants. It is loud with insects, birds, and the movement of animals through undergrowth. It is one of the most complex ecosystems in the world.

image.note: Illustration: aerial view of rainforest canopy, stretching to horizon with river cutting through

pages.text: A rainforest is a forest that receives very high rainfall throughout the year, typically more than 2,000 millimetres annually. Nigerian rainforest receives between 1,500 and 3,000 millimetres of rain each year. That rain, combined with the constant heat of the tropics, produces conditions where plants grow with extraordinary speed and density, layering on top of each other in the competition for sunlight.

Nigeria's rainforest once covered a much larger area than it does today. Centuries of farming, and decades of intensive logging and development, have reduced it dramatically. What remains is fragmented: pockets and corridors of forest separated by farmland, roads, and towns. The largest continuous area of rainforest in Nigeria is now in the south-east, in Cross River State.

Stand still in the rainforest for one minute and count what you hear. A hornbill's wingbeats, heavy as a fan. The whoop of a mona monkey troop. Cicadas in shifting waves. Water dripping from leaf to leaf long after the rain has stopped. The forest is never silent, and researchers can identify dozens of species without seeing a single animal, simply by listening. Sound is the forest's second language.
A rainforest is not one thing. It is a series of distinct layers, each with its own light levels, temperature, humidity, and community of living things.

image.note: Detailed diagram showing forest floor, understorey, canopy, and emergent layer with representative species at each level

pages.text: The forest floor is the darkest layer. Almost no direct sunlight reaches it. It is covered in dead leaves, fallen branches, and decomposing matter. Fungi, beetles, termites, and other decomposers break this material down and return its nutrients to the soil. Larger animals, including forest elephants and forest buffaloes, move through this layer.

The understorey is the layer of shrubs, ferns, and young trees that grow in the dim light between the forest floor and the canopy above. Many of Nigeria's most important medicinal plants grow here. It is also the home of many frog and lizard species, adapted to the low light and high humidity.

The canopy is the main layer of the forest: a dense ceiling of interlocking branches and leaves, between 20 and 40 metres above the ground. This is where most of the forest's animal life is concentrated. Monkeys, birds, squirrels, and hundreds of insect species live, feed, and breed in the canopy, rarely descending to the ground.

Above the canopy, occasional trees push even higher, their crowns rising above the general ceiling to catch full sunlight. These emergent trees can reach 60 metres or more. Eagles nest in them. Their isolated crowns, exposed to wind that does not penetrate below, have a different microclimate from the rest of the forest.

The rainforest is also a pharmacy. Nigerian healers have drawn medicines from forest plants for centuries: bark for fevers, leaves for wounds, roots for stomach ailments. Modern science keeps confirming what tradition knew. Compounds from West African forest plants are being studied for treating malaria, diabetes, and infections. Every hectare of forest cleared may contain an undiscovered treatment, burned before anyone knew it existed. That possibility alone argues for keeping the forest standing.

Seed dispersal is the forest's quiet engineering. A hornbill swallows a fruit whole, flies two kilometres, and deposits the seed, neatly fertilised, far from the parent tree. Elephants do the same on a grander scale: some large forest seeds germinate poorly unless they have passed through an elephant. Kill the animals and the forest slowly stops moving. Botanists call this the empty forest problem: trees still standing, but the system that renews them gone.

The species diversity of a tropical rainforest is almost beyond comprehension. A single hectare of Nigerian rainforest may contain more tree species than exist in the whole of the United Kingdom. The insects are so numerous and so varied that scientists have barely begun to catalogue them.

Plants in the rainforest compete intensely for light. Some climb other trees using tendrils and suckers. Some grow directly on the branches of larger trees, drawing nutrients from the air and rain rather than the soil. These epiphytes, or air plants, cover the branches of canopy trees in the wetter parts of the forest, adding another layer of life to the already dense community above.

image.note: Illustration of a canopy branch covered in epiphytes, mosses, and small ferns

pages.text: The relationship between animals and plants in a rainforest is extraordinarily close. Many trees depend on specific animals to pollinate their flowers or carry their seeds to new locations. Some fruits are eaten only by particular bird or primate species, which then disperse the seeds in their droppings. Remove the animal, and the tree cannot reproduce. Remove the tree, and the animal loses its food source. The forest is a web of dependencies.

The fig tree is one of the most important trees in the Nigerian rainforest. Different species of fig fruit at different times of year, providing a continuous supply of food even in seasons when other fruits are scarce. More than one thousand species of animal are known to eat figs across West Africa. The fig tree is sometimes called the keystone species of the rainforest, because so much of the forest community depends on it.

People are part of this forest too. Communities such as the Ekuri in Cross River State have managed their communal forest for generations, harvesting carefully and refusing to sell out to loggers. Their forest remains rich while surrounding areas have been stripped. The lesson is not that people must leave forests alone. It is that forests survive where the people who live closest to them hold real power over what happens to them.

Bushmeat is the forest's hardest question. Hunting wild animals for food is ancient, and for many rural families it remains an important source of protein and income. But modern roads, guns, and city markets have multiplied the pressure far beyond what forests can bear. Endangered species end up in cooking pots hundreds of kilometres from where they were shot. Solving this requires alternatives, not lectures: affordable protein, real livelihoods, and enforcement aimed at traffickers rather than hungry villagers.

Nigeria has one of the highest rates of deforestation in the world. The country has lost more than ninety percent of its original forest cover. The causes are well understood: logging for timber, clearing for agriculture, charcoal production, and the expansion of oil palm plantations. What was once one of West Africa's largest continuous forest belts is now fragmented and shrinking.

The consequences are serious. Deforestation releases stored carbon into the atmosphere, contributing to climate change. It destroys the habitats of animals and plants, many of which have no alternatives. It increases soil erosion, as tree roots that held the soil in place are removed. It reduces rainfall, as forests generate their own rain through transpiration, the release of water vapour from leaves.

pages.text: The Cross River National Park in south-eastern Nigeria protects one of the most significant remaining areas of Nigerian rainforest. It is the habitat of the Cross River gorilla and many other endangered species. It is also home to communities who have lived in and around the forest for generations, and whose relationship with it is complex.

Protecting the rainforest is not simply a matter of locking it away. It requires finding ways for people to benefit from the living forest without destroying it: through sustainable forestry, through ecotourism, through payments for the environmental services the forest provides. These approaches are being developed and tested in Nigeria and across the region. Their success or failure will determine the future of one of Africa's most important ecosystems.

There is hope, and it has an address. The Obudu Plateau and the forests of Cross River State draw visitors from across Nigeria and beyond, proving that a standing forest can earn a living. Community forest projects, gorilla guardians recruited from villages that once hunted, and replanting schemes led by young Nigerians are all growing. The Nigerian rainforest has lost most of its area but none of its importance. What remains is worth everything it will take to keep it.
